modules.name: Module 1: Communication Foundations
modules.desc: Week 1 review — what communication is, speech vs. language, the communication framework, the process/subsystems of speech production, the Bloom & Lahey taxonomy, the speech chain, and the auditory feedback loop.

modules.name: Module 2: Defining the Roles of SLPAs
modules.desc: Scope of practice, minimum qualifications, supervision (ASHA & California), ethics/Code of Conduct, work settings, and duties of the speech-language pathology assistant.

modules.name: Module 4: Therapy Approaches, HIPAA & Communication Milestones
modules.desc: Clinician-directed vs. naturalistic therapy approaches; HIPAA and patient confidentiality for SLPA students/interns; and developmental communication milestones (Oller, Sander, phonological processes, Brown's MLU stages, red flags).

modules.name: Module 5: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy
modules.desc: Clinical strategies universal across treatment: task analysis and scaffolding, linguistic and social complexity, modeling, prompting and cuing, and feedback — anchored in the ZPD and the Four Essential Clinical Supports.

glossary.def: A model of the supervisory relationship that moves across three stages — Evaluation-Feedback, Transitional, and Self-Supervision — with supervisory style shifting from Direct/Active to Collaborative to Consultative as the supervisee gains competence.
glossary.source: Anderson (1988), The Supervisory Process in SLP & Audiology

glossary.def: The production of speech sounds ("the producers of speech sounds"), carried out by the lips, teeth, tongue, alveolar ridge, hard palate, soft palate, and mandible. One of the four components of speech.
glossary.source: Hulit, Fahey & Howard (2015), Born to Talk

glossary.def: The set of principles and rules of ethical practice for certified assistants, built on three principles: responsibility to persons served, responsibility to the public, and responsibility for professional relationships.
glossary.source: ASHA (2020), Assistants Code of Conduct

glossary.def: A cue delivered through sound (e.g., a verbal hint or emphasized sound).
glossary.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

glossary.def: The self-monitoring cycle of speech: I say it → I hear it → I process it → I modify it.
glossary.source: Module 1 Review (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: An SLPA who, with adequate training, may interpret/translate during screening and assessment (exclusive of interpretation of results) and provide services in another language under SLP supervision (e.g., Susan).
glossary.source: Kimball & Charboneau, A Day in the Life of an SLPA (Resource Manual, Appendix 1-D)

glossary.def: A model describing language as three intersecting dimensions: Form, Content, and Use.
glossary.source: Bloom & Lahey (Taxonomy of Language)

glossary.def: Brown's five stages linking age, MLU, and grammatical milestones: Stage I (12-26mo, MLU 1.0-2.0) through Stage V+ (47+mo, MLU 4.5+).
glossary.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

glossary.def: Certified Speech-Language Pathology Assistant — the credential earned through ASHA's Assistants Certification Program (launched December 2020).
glossary.source: ASHA (2022), SLPA Scope of Practice

glossary.def: Oller's Stage 4 (7-9 months): CV syllables with adult-like timing, including reduplicated syllables like /baba/ and /mama/.
glossary.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

glossary.def: Certificate of Clinical Competence in Speech-Language Pathology, awarded by ASHA. Required (and/or state licensure) for an SLP to supervise an SLPA.
glossary.source: Module 2: Defining SLPA (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: A minimum 9-month period of mentored professional experience completed after graduate coursework; a supervising SLP must have completed the CFY plus additional experience before supervising an SLPA.
glossary.source: Module 2: Defining SLPA (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: A therapy approach in which the clinician controls the session — choosing activities, targets, reinforcers, and what counts as a successful response — and elicits specific (imitative or spontaneous) responses. Strategies include drill and drill play.
glossary.source: An Overview of Tx Approaches (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: A phonological process: omitting one or more consonants in a cluster (e.g., clean → /kin/). Without /s/: gone by ~4; with /s/: gone by ~5. Persists after 3.
glossary.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

glossary.def: The process of exchanging information, ideas, thoughts, and feelings between individuals. Communication can be intended or unintended, and communication methods are ever-changing.
glossary.source: Module 1 Review (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: The dimension of language covering semantics (meaning).
glossary.source: Bloom & Lahey (Taxonomy of Language)

glossary.def: Credit for continuing education; requirements vary by state (e.g., Florida requires 20 CEU per biennium for renewal).
glossary.source: Kimball & Charboneau, A Day in the Life of an SLPA (Resource Manual, Appendix 1-D)

glossary.def: Ongoing training SLPAs complete to maintain credentials; in California SLPAs complete 12 hours of CPD every 2 years.
glossary.source: Kimball & Charboneau, A Day in the Life of an SLPA (Resource Manual, Appendix 1-D)

glossary.def: Feedback that guides the client to fix an error; most effective when specific and descriptive (e.g., 'Oops, your tongue came between your teeth — can you put it back up top?').
glossary.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

glossary.def: A hint that helps the client be successful; cues can be visual, auditory, or tactile. Clinicians start with frequent, varied cues and fade to occasional, subtler ones.
glossary.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

glossary.def: Removing information that identifies an individual (names, site references) from notes/logs so that client privacy is protected — required when taking observation notes.
glossary.source: HIPAA: Patient Confidentiality (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: Language practiced apart from natural communicative context — a limitation of the clinician-directed approach that can make generalization difficult.
glossary.source: An Overview of Tx Approaches (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: In-view (on-site or live/synchronous telesupervision) observation and guidance while the SLPA is performing a clinical activity, allowing immediate feedback. Reviewing a recorded session later does NOT count as direct supervision.
glossary.source: ASHA (2022), SLPA Scope of Practice

glossary.def: A clinician-directed strategy using many structured repetitions of a target.
glossary.source: An Overview of Tx Approaches (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: A clinician-directed strategy that adds a playful/motivating element to structured drill.
glossary.source: An Overview of Tx Approaches (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: Services for children birth to age 3, often delivered through home visits with naturalistic, child-centered therapy and parent coaching.
glossary.source: Module 2: Defining SLPA (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: The first stage of Anderson's continuum, paired with a Direct/Active supervisory style; the supervisor leads and provides substantial direction and feedback.
glossary.source: Anderson (1988), The Supervisory Process in SLP & Audiology

glossary.def: The production side of language — conveying messages through speaking and writing.
glossary.source: Module 1 Review (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: Gradually reducing supports (models, prompts, cues, feedback) as the client's accuracy and independence increase.
glossary.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

glossary.def: Information given to the client about their performance. Most effective feedback is specific, succinct/quick, and followed by an immediate opportunity to practice; begin with copious feedback and fade to occasional, subtle forms.
glossary.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

glossary.def: A phonological process: omitting a singleton consonant at the end of a word (e.g., cat → /kæ/). Typically gone by ~3 years.
glossary.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

glossary.def: The rate, rhythm, and continuity (smooth flow) of speech. One of the four components of speech.
glossary.source: Module 1 Review (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: A naturalistic strategy in which the clinician repeatedly models a target form in meaningful contexts.
glossary.source: An Overview of Tx Approaches (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: The dimension of language covering syntax, morphology, and phonology.
glossary.source: Bloom & Lahey (Taxonomy of Language)

glossary.def: Under California regulation, at least 30 hours per week. An SLP is recommended to supervise no more than three FTE SLPAs.
glossary.source: CA Code of Regs, Title 16 §1399.170 et seq. (Article 12)

glossary.def: Carryover of a learned skill to new contexts; the naturalistic approach supports it well (especially in later therapy stages), while it is harder with clinician-directed drill.
glossary.source: An Overview of Tx Approaches (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: A phonological process: substituting /w/ or /j/ for another consonant, typically a liquid (e.g., run → /wʌn/). Gliding of initial liquids typically gone by ~7 years.
glossary.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

glossary.def: The smallest meaningful unit that signals grammatical meaning (e.g., present progressive -ing, plural -s, possessive -'s, past tense -ed); emerge in Brown's Stage II onward.
glossary.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

glossary.def: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act — passed in 1996 and updated in 2003 to improve the flow of patient health information while protecting patients' privacy rights.
glossary.source: HIPAA: Patient Confidentiality (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: A written plan of care used in school settings; SLPAs prepare materials for and support IEP meetings but do not write or modify the plan.
glossary.source: Kimball & Charboneau, A Day in the Life of an SLPA (Resource Manual, Appendix 1-D)

glossary.def: The early-intervention counterpart to the IEP for children birth to 3 and their families.
glossary.source: Kimball & Charboneau, A Day in the Life of an SLPA (Resource Manual, Appendix 1-D)

glossary.def: Under California regulation, the level of supervision required for direct client activity involving medically fragile patients; the SLPA acts only under the direction of the supervisor, who must be present.
glossary.source: CA Code of Regs, Title 16 §1399.170 et seq. (Article 12)

glossary.def: A naturalistic strategy in which the clinician models language around the child's focus without demanding a response.
glossary.source: An Overview of Tx Approaches (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: Monitoring or reviewing the SLPA's activities without being physically present or available in real time — e.g., reviewing demonstration videos, client files, or recorded sessions, and conducting supervisory conferences by phone or secure virtual meeting.
glossary.source: ASHA (2022), SLPA Scope of Practice

glossary.def: A rule-based cognitive system of symbols used for communicating. Language has both expressive and receptive components, is governed primarily by left-hemisphere brain structures, and is learned.
glossary.source: Module 1 Review (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: The larynx, which serves as the sound source (voice) for speech.
glossary.source: Kent (1997), The Speech Sciences

glossary.def: The complexity of the language being used in a task; one dimension a clinician adjusts when building a hierarchy of tasks.
glossary.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

glossary.def: The average number of morphemes per utterance; a reliable predictor of language complexity that increases ~1.2 morphemes/year from 18 months to age 5 (Owens, 1996).
glossary.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

glossary.def: Describes an acutely ill patient in an unstable health condition. Treatment of a medically fragile client by an SLPA requires 100% direct supervision by the SLP.
glossary.source: ASHA (2022), SLPA Scope of Practice

glossary.def: A naturalistic strategy that embeds brief teaching episodes in the natural environment following the child's lead.
glossary.source: An Overview of Tx Approaches (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: The HIPAA principle of accessing only the medical/background information needed to perform one's job.
glossary.source: HIPAA: Patient Confidentiality (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: Demonstrating a target behavior for the client. Variants include modeling with emphasis, modeling for direct imitation, and modeling for delayed imitation; begin with constant models and fade to occasional, then fade completely.
glossary.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

glossary.def: The clinician models a target that the client is expected to reproduce after a delay rather than immediately.
glossary.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

glossary.def: The clinician models a target immediately before the client is expected to imitate it.
glossary.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

glossary.def: The study of word structure and morphemes (the smallest units of meaning). A component of Form in the Bloom & Lahey taxonomy.
glossary.source: Module 1 Review (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: The nerve pathways that carry signals from the brain (the "computer center") out to the muscles of speech.
glossary.source: Hulit, Fahey & Howard (2015), Born to Talk

glossary.def: California requires an SLPA to display their name and registration status on a name tag in at least 18-point type while working, and to self-identify as an SLPA.
glossary.source: CA Code of Regs, Title 16 §1399.170 et seq. (Article 12)

glossary.def: A therapy approach delivered in the natural environment following typical communication patterns, where the client helps select activities and the clinician models/stresses targets with no demand for a response. Strategies include indirect language stimulation, milieu teaching, script therapy, and focused language stimulation.
glossary.source: An Overview of Tx Approaches (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: Child-centered, play-based therapy delivered in natural settings such as the home, common in early intervention.
glossary.source: Kimball & Charboneau, A Day in the Life of an SLPA (Resource Manual, Appendix 1-D)

glossary.def: General evaluative feedback that does not describe the behavior (e.g., 'Good job,' 'Nope, not opposites').
glossary.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

glossary.def: Oller (1980) describes five stages of early vocal development: (1) Phonation (birth-1mo), (2) Cooing/Gooing (2-3mo), (3) Exploration/Expansion (4-6mo), (4) Canonical babbling (7-9mo), (5) Variegated babbling (10-12mo).
glossary.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

glossary.def: "The noise source" of speech, produced by vibration of the vocal folds of the larynx.
glossary.source: Hulit, Fahey & Howard (2015), Born to Talk

glossary.def: A systematic, rule-governed simplification of adult speech sound patterns in child speech (e.g., fronting, stopping, cluster reduction).
glossary.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

glossary.def: The sound system of a language and the rules governing how speech sounds are organized and combined. A component of speech and part of Form in the Bloom & Lahey taxonomy.
glossary.source: Module 1 Review (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: A written service plan (e.g., IEP, IFSP, treatment plan) developed and monitored by the supervising SLP; the SLPA implements it but may not write, develop, or modify it.
glossary.source: ASHA (2022), SLPA Scope of Practice

glossary.def: The social use of language in context (also called discourse). In the Bloom & Lahey taxonomy, pragmatics is the Use dimension.
glossary.source: Module 1 Review (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: Collecting, graphing, and reviewing data on a client's target skills to gauge response to treatment. SLPAs may administer/score progress-monitoring tools but not interpret them.
glossary.source: ASHA (2022), SLPA Scope of Practice

glossary.def: A question or direction for the client to respond to. Clinicians begin by constantly prompting and fade to occasional, more subtle prompts.
glossary.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

glossary.def: Patient/client/student health and background information that must be kept confidential; SLPAs access only what they need to do their job and secure all files.
glossary.source: HIPAA: Patient Confidentiality (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: A service-delivery model in which the SLPA works with students individually or in small groups outside the classroom.
glossary.source: Module 2: Defining SLPA (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: A service-delivery model in which services are provided inside the classroom (e.g., in self-contained classrooms).
glossary.source: Module 2: Defining SLPA (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: The comprehension side of language — understanding through listening and reading.
glossary.source: Module 1 Review (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: Warning signs of possible speech/language problems at given ages (e.g., no babbling by 9mo, not pointing by 12mo, no first word by 15mo, vocabulary <50 words at 24mo, strangers can't understand at 36mo).
glossary.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

glossary.def: Repeating the same CV syllable (e.g., /baba/); characteristic of canonical babbling.
glossary.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

glossary.def: A phonological process: repeating phonemes or syllables (e.g., bottle → /bɔbɔ/). Disappears by ~3 years.
glossary.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

glossary.def: "The tone shapers" of speech, occurring in the pharynx, mouth, and nasal cavities.
glossary.source: Hulit, Fahey & Howard (2015), Born to Talk

glossary.def: In speech production, "the power supply." Inhalation uses the thoracic muscles and exhalation uses the abdominal muscles to provide the airflow that powers speech.
glossary.source: Hulit, Fahey & Howard (2015), Born to Talk

glossary.def: The trachea and lungs, which supply the breath support that powers speech.
glossary.source: Kent (1997), The Speech Sciences

glossary.def: Sander (1972): nasals (m, n, ng) and stops (p, b, t, d, k, g) and glides (w, y) are acquired earliest, followed by fricatives (f, v, s, z, sh, zh) and voiced/voiceless 'th', affricates (ch, j), then liquids (l, r). Voiced/voiceless 'th' are generally the latest phonemes.
glossary.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

glossary.def: Support provided in incremental steps to help someone learn a new skill; supports are faded as accuracy increases.
glossary.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

glossary.def: The defined set of responsibilities, duties, and functions that an SLPA may perform (and those they may not), as set by ASHA and by state regulation. For California SLPAs, scope is governed by ASHA's SLPA Scope of Practice and Title 16, Article 12 of the CA Code of Regulations.
glossary.source: Module 2: Defining SLPA (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: A pass-fail procedure to identify individuals who may need further assessment. An SLPA may administer and score screenings, but clinical interpretation is done by the SLP.
glossary.source: ASHA (2022), SLPA Scope of Practice

glossary.def: A naturalistic strategy using familiar, predictable event routines (scripts) to support language.
glossary.source: An Overview of Tx Approaches (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: The final stage of Anderson's continuum, paired with a Consultative style; the supervisee self-monitors and the supervisor consults as needed.
glossary.source: Anderson (1988), The Supervisory Process in SLP & Audiology

glossary.def: The study of meaning in language (words and sentences). In the Bloom & Lahey taxonomy, semantics is the Content dimension.
glossary.source: Module 1 Review (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: The nerve pathways that carry feedback from the speech mechanism and ear back to the brain.
glossary.source: Hulit, Fahey & Howard (2015), Born to Talk

glossary.def: A Subjective, Objective, Assessment, and Plan progress note written after a session to document client responses and goals (e.g., Stephanie's daily documentation).
glossary.source: Kimball & Charboneau, A Day in the Life of an SLPA (Resource Manual, Appendix 1-D)

glossary.def: The complexity of the setting/social context of a task; one dimension a clinician adjusts when building a hierarchy of tasks.
glossary.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

glossary.def: Feedback that describes exactly what the client did (e.g., 'You put your tongue behind your front teeth and that /s/ came right out'), as opposed to non-specific evaluative feedback like 'Good job.'
glossary.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

glossary.def: The physiological (motor) act of producing and manipulating sound; often defined as "the oral expression of language." Speech relies on the lungs, larynx, and oral and nasal structures, and is generally considered innate.
glossary.source: Module 1 Review (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: Typical percentage of speech understood by an unfamiliar listener by age: 19-24mo = 25-50%; 2-3yr = 50-75%; 4-5yr = 75-90%; 5+yr = 90-100% (Peña-Brooks & Hegde, 2007).
glossary.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

glossary.def: Support personnel who, after academic coursework, clinical practicum, and credentialing, perform tasks prescribed, directed, and supervised by an ASHA-certified and/or state-credentialed SLP. An SLPA is not an independent practitioner and never carries their own caseload.
glossary.source: ASHA (2022), SLPA Scope of Practice

glossary.def: SLPA entry requirements differ by state — e.g., California accepts an associate's (SLPA-accredited/board-approved) OR a bachelor's in CSD/SLP; other states specify their own degree, practicum, and supervision rules.
glossary.source: Kimball & Charboneau, A Day in the Life of an SLPA (Resource Manual, Appendix 1-D)

glossary.def: A phonological process: substituting a stop for a fricative, liquid, nasal, or glide (e.g., sun → /dʌn/). Persists after 3.
glossary.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

glossary.def: The ASHA-certified and/or state-licensed speech-language pathologist who retains full legal and ethical responsibility for all students, patients, and clients, delegates appropriate tasks to the SLPA, and provides direct and indirect supervision.
glossary.source: ASHA (2022), SLPA Scope of Practice

glossary.def: The upper airway (pharyngeal-oral-nasal system) used in speech production, including the nasal cavity, oral cavity, pharyngeal cavity, lips, tongue, and jaw.
glossary.source: Kent (1997), The Speech Sciences

glossary.def: The rules governing word order and sentence structure. A component of Form in the Bloom & Lahey taxonomy.
glossary.source: Module 1 Review (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

glossary.def: A cue delivered through touch (e.g., a touch to the face to support a sound).
glossary.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

glossary.def: Breaking a complex task down into smaller, more manageable steps (e.g., to spell your name: learn letters → learn the letters in your name → trace the letters → spell on your own).
glossary.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

glossary.def: An ordered sequence of tasks (varying linguistic and social complexity) the client works to master as part of a goal.
glossary.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

glossary.def: Supervision in which the SLP views and communicates with the SLPA (and client) in real time via telecommunication technology, enabling immediate feedback. Counts as direct supervision; reviewing a recording later does not.
glossary.source: ASHA (2022), SLPA Scope of Practice

glossary.def: Denes & Pinson's model describing the different forms a spoken message takes as it travels from the speaker's mind to the listener's mind, passing through linguistic, physiological, and acoustic levels.
glossary.source: Denes & Pinson (1973), The Speech Chain

glossary.def: The middle stage of Anderson's continuum, paired with a Collaborative style; supervisor and supervisee share responsibility as competence grows.
glossary.source: Anderson (1988), The Supervisory Process in SLP & Audiology

glossary.def: The dimension of language covering pragmatics and discourse (social use).
glossary.source: Bloom & Lahey (Taxonomy of Language)

glossary.def: Oller's Stage 5 (10-12 months): different CV syllables combined (e.g., /bamaga/), with adult-like intonation and prosody.
glossary.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

glossary.def: A phonological process: substituting a front sound for a back (velar) sound (e.g., can → /tæn/). Fronting of initial velars typically gone by ~4 years.
glossary.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

glossary.def: A cue delivered through sight (e.g., a gesture, picture, or written support).
glossary.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

glossary.def: The vocal characteristics produced by the larynx, including pitch, loudness, and quality. One of the four components of speech.
glossary.source: Module 1 Review (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

flashcards.front: What are the four components of SPEECH in the communication framework?
flashcards.back: Articulation, Phonology, Fluency, and Voice.
flashcards.source: Module 1 Review (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

flashcards.front: What are the four components of LANGUAGE in the communication framework?
flashcards.back: Semantics, Morphology, Syntax, and Pragmatics.
flashcards.source: Module 1 Review (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

flashcards.front: Speech vs. Language: which is a physiological process and which is a cognitive process?
flashcards.back: Speech is a physiological (motor) process; language is a cognitive process.
flashcards.source: Module 1 Review (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

flashcards.front: Speech is described as "innate"; language is described as ___.
flashcards.back: Learned. (Speech = innate; language = learned.)
flashcards.source: Module 1 Review (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

flashcards.front: What are the two components of receptive language?
flashcards.back: Listening and reading (comprehension).
flashcards.source: Module 1 Review (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

flashcards.front: What are the two components of expressive language?
flashcards.back: Speaking and writing (production).
flashcards.source: Module 1 Review (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

flashcards.front: List the four subsystems of speech production from power source upward.
flashcards.back: Respiration (power supply) → Phonation (noise source) → Resonation (tone shapers) → Articulation (producers of speech sounds).
flashcards.source: Hulit, Fahey & Howard (2015), Born to Talk

flashcards.front: In the Process of Speech, what is the role of RESPIRATION?
flashcards.back: The power supply — inhalation via thoracic muscles, exhalation via abdominal muscles.
flashcards.source: Hulit, Fahey & Howard (2015), Born to Talk

flashcards.front: In the Process of Speech, what is the role of PHONATION?
flashcards.back: The noise source — vibration of the vocal folds of the larynx.
flashcards.source: Hulit, Fahey & Howard (2015), Born to Talk

flashcards.front: In the Process of Speech, what is the role of RESONATION?
flashcards.back: The tone shapers — pharynx, mouth, and nasal cavities.
flashcards.source: Hulit, Fahey & Howard (2015), Born to Talk

flashcards.front: In the Process of Speech, what is the role of ARTICULATION?
flashcards.back: The producers of speech sounds — lips, teeth, tongue, alveolar ridge, hard palate, soft palate, and mandible.
flashcards.source: Hulit, Fahey & Howard (2015), Born to Talk

flashcards.front: What three dimensions make up the Bloom & Lahey Taxonomy of Language?
flashcards.back: Form, Content, and Use.
flashcards.source: Bloom & Lahey (Taxonomy of Language)

flashcards.front: Bloom & Lahey: what falls under FORM?
flashcards.back: Syntax, morphology, and phonology.
flashcards.source: Bloom & Lahey (Taxonomy of Language)

flashcards.front: Bloom & Lahey: what falls under CONTENT?
flashcards.back: Semantics (meaning).
flashcards.source: Bloom & Lahey (Taxonomy of Language)

flashcards.front: Bloom & Lahey: what falls under USE?
flashcards.back: Pragmatics / discourse.
flashcards.source: Bloom & Lahey (Taxonomy of Language)

flashcards.front: What three subsystems of speech production are shown in Kent's (1997) supralaryngeal diagram?
flashcards.back: The supralaryngeal (pharyngeal-oral-nasal) system, the laryngeal system, and the respiratory system.
flashcards.source: Kent (1997), The Speech Sciences

flashcards.front: What are the four steps of the auditory feedback loop?
flashcards.back: I say it → I hear it → I process it → I modify it.
flashcards.source: Module 1 Review (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

flashcards.front: In the Speech Chain (Denes & Pinson), what levels does a message pass through from speaker to listener?
flashcards.back: Linguistic → Physiological → Acoustic → Physiological → Linguistic level.
flashcards.source: Denes & Pinson (1973), The Speech Chain

flashcards.front: Communication can be intended or ___.
flashcards.back: Unintended.
flashcards.source: Module 1 Review (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

flashcards.front: What are the minimum qualifications for an SLP to SUPERVISE an SLPA?
flashcards.back: Hold the ASHA CCC-SLP (and/or state license); completed the 9-month CFY plus experience; at least 2 hours of continuing education in clinical instruction/supervision; and adherence to state supervision laws.
flashcards.source: Module 2: Defining SLPA (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

flashcards.front: What are the three STAGES of Anderson's Continuum of Supervision?
flashcards.back: Evaluation-Feedback → Transitional → Self-Supervision.
flashcards.source: Anderson (1988), The Supervisory Process in SLP & Audiology

flashcards.front: What are the three STYLES in Anderson's Continuum, and how do they map to the stages?
flashcards.back: Direct/Active (Evaluation-Feedback) → Collaborative (Transitional) → Consultative (Self-Supervision).
flashcards.source: Anderson (1988), The Supervisory Process in SLP & Audiology

flashcards.front: Define DIRECT supervision. Does reviewing a recorded session count?
flashcards.back: In-view observation and guidance while the SLPA performs a clinical activity (on-site or live telesupervision), allowing immediate feedback. Reviewing a recorded session later does NOT count as direct supervision.
flashcards.source: ASHA (2022), SLPA Scope of Practice

flashcards.front: Define INDIRECT supervision. Give two examples.
flashcards.back: Monitoring the SLPA's work without being present in real time — e.g., reviewing client files, reviewing recorded sessions, or holding supervisory conferences by phone/secure virtual meeting.
flashcards.source: ASHA (2022), SLPA Scope of Practice

flashcards.front: California: how much DIRECT supervision is required in the first 90 days after initial licensure?
flashcards.back: At least 20% per week of the SLPA's work schedule (on-site observation and guidance) for the first 90 days following initial licensure.
flashcards.source: CA Code of Regs, Title 16 §1399.170 et seq. (Article 12)

flashcards.front: What level of supervision is required when an SLPA treats a MEDICALLY FRAGILE client?
flashcards.back: 100% direct supervision by the SLP.
flashcards.source: ASHA (2022), SLPA Scope of Practice

flashcards.front: May an SLPA perform tasks when the supervising SLP cannot be reached?
flashcards.back: No. An SLPA may not perform tasks when the supervising SLP cannot be reached by personal contact (phone, pager, or other immediate/electronic means).
flashcards.source: Module 2: Defining SLPA (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

flashcards.front: Name four tasks that are WITHIN an SLPA's scope of practice.
flashcards.back: Examples: administering/scoring screenings (no interpretation); implementing the SLP's plan of care; providing direct therapy on SLP-developed goals; collecting/documenting data; programming AAC devices; assisting with clerical duties.
flashcards.source: ASHA (2022), SLPA Scope of Practice

flashcards.front: Name four tasks OUTSIDE an SLPA's scope of practice.
flashcards.back: Examples: diagnosing disorders; interpreting assessments; writing/modifying the plan of care; making referrals; discharging a client; signing documents without the SLP's co-signature; representing themselves as the SLP.
flashcards.source: ASHA (2022), SLPA Scope of Practice

flashcards.front: What are the three Principles of Conduct in the ASHA Assistants Code of Conduct?
flashcards.back: (1) Responsibility to persons served professionally; (2) Responsibility to the public; (3) Responsibility for professional relationships.
flashcards.source: ASHA (2020), Assistants Code of Conduct

flashcards.front: In what work settings do SLPAs practice?
flashcards.back: Public schools (pre-K, K-8, HS, ATP), private clinics (1:1 and small group), and early intervention (birth-3, home visits) — among hospitals, SNFs, and home health.
flashcards.source: Module 2: Defining SLPA (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

flashcards.front: List core DUTIES of an SLPA.
flashcards.back: Read/understand goals; plan goal-targeted activities; provide therapy (1:1, small group, push-in); document services; manage materials; support the SLP with clerical duties (progress reports, IEP paperwork); coordinate with teachers/parents.
flashcards.source: Module 2: Defining SLPA (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

flashcards.front: California name-tag rule for SLPAs?
flashcards.back: The SLPA must display name and registration status on a name tag in at least 18-point type and self-identify as an SLPA.
flashcards.source: CA Code of Regs, Title 16 §1399.170 et seq. (Article 12)

flashcards.front: Under CA regulation, what are the three TYPES of supervision?
flashcards.back: Immediate (medically fragile / new direct client activity), Direct (new screening/treatment activity the SLPA has been trained on but not yet performed in client care), and Indirect (previously-instructed tasks, clerical, non-client-care).
flashcards.source: CA Code of Regs, Title 16 §1399.170 et seq. (Article 12)

flashcards.front: Who retains legal and ethical responsibility for the client — the SLPA or the SLP?
flashcards.back: The supervising SLP always retains full legal and ethical responsibility; it cannot be delegated.
flashcards.source: ASHA (2022), SLPA Scope of Practice

flashcards.front: How many FTE SLPAs is an SLP recommended to supervise, and what is an FTE in CA?
flashcards.back: No more than three (3) full-time-equivalent SLPAs; in California an FTE is at least 30 hours per week.
flashcards.source: CA Code of Regs, Title 16 §1399.170 et seq. (Article 12)

flashcards.front: Can an SLPA interpret assessment results or diagnose?
flashcards.back: No. SLPAs may administer and score assessments/screenings (if trained and competent) but interpretation, diagnosis, and eligibility determination are exclusive to the SLP.
flashcards.source: ASHA (2022), SLPA Scope of Practice

flashcards.front: In California, how much continuing professional development must an SLPA complete?
flashcards.back: 12 hours of CPD every 2 years (per the 'Day in the Life' profile of Jackie).
flashcards.source: Kimball & Charboneau, A Day in the Life of an SLPA (Resource Manual, Appendix 1-D)

flashcards.front: What is a SOAP note and when is it written?
flashcards.back: A Subjective-Objective-Assessment-Plan progress note documenting a client's session responses and goals, written after each session.
flashcards.source: Kimball & Charboneau, A Day in the Life of an SLPA (Resource Manual, Appendix 1-D)

flashcards.front: What may a BILINGUAL SLPA do that adds to the standard scope?
flashcards.back: With training, assist with interpretation/translation during screening and assessment (not interpreting results) and provide services in another language under SLP supervision.
flashcards.source: Kimball & Charboneau, A Day in the Life of an SLPA (Resource Manual, Appendix 1-D)

flashcards.front: Across the 'Day in the Life' profiles, what varies most from state to state?
flashcards.back: Entry/licensure requirements (degree type, practicum hours, supervision rules) and continuing-education requirements.
flashcards.source: Kimball & Charboneau, A Day in the Life of an SLPA (Resource Manual, Appendix 1-D)

flashcards.front: What settings appear across the SLPA profiles?
flashcards.back: Home/early-intervention, Head Start/daycare, private practice, and public schools (K-8, elementary, secondary).
flashcards.source: Kimball & Charboneau, A Day in the Life of an SLPA (Resource Manual, Appendix 1-D)

flashcards.front: What common 'words of wisdom' recur across the SLPA profiles?
flashcards.back: Know your scope of practice, keep learning/observe other clinicians, don't give up, ask questions, and specialize to set yourself apart.
flashcards.source: Kimball & Charboneau, A Day in the Life of an SLPA (Resource Manual, Appendix 1-D)

flashcards.front: What characterizes the CLINICIAN-DIRECTED approach?
flashcards.back: The clinician controls the session — chooses activities, targets, reinforcers, and defines a successful response — and elicits specific imitative or spontaneous responses (drill, drill play).
flashcards.source: An Overview of Tx Approaches (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

flashcards.front: What characterizes the NATURALISTIC approach?
flashcards.back: Therapy in the natural environment following typical communication patterns; the client helps select activities; the clinician models/stresses targets with no demand for a response (indirect language stimulation, milieu teaching, script therapy, focused language stimulation).
flashcards.source: An Overview of Tx Approaches (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

flashcards.front: Advantages of the clinician-directed approach?
flashcards.back: Good for introducing/teaching a new skill; efficient (many repetitions); easier to plan and take data; works well for articulation, phonology, morphology, and syntax.
flashcards.source: An Overview of Tx Approaches (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

flashcards.front: Disadvantages of the clinician-directed approach?
flashcards.back: Some clients can't tolerate it; doesn't follow typical communication patterns; language is decontextualized; generalization is difficult; not great for semantics, pragmatics, fluency.
flashcards.source: An Overview of Tx Approaches (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

flashcards.front: Advantages of the naturalistic approach?
flashcards.back: Motivation, sustained attention, treatment efficacy, caregiver participation/coaching, strong generalization (great for later stages), and good for semantics/pragmatics (contextualized).
flashcards.source: An Overview of Tx Approaches (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

flashcards.front: Disadvantages of the naturalistic approach?
flashcards.back: Less efficient at targeting specific responses; hard to get repetitions; hard to plan and take data; not great for initial stages of articulation/phonology therapy.
flashcards.source: An Overview of Tx Approaches (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

flashcards.front: What four factors help you CHOOSE a therapy approach?
flashcards.back: Age of the client, social abilities of the client, goals, and where the client is in the therapeutic process.
flashcards.source: An Overview of Tx Approaches (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

flashcards.front: What does HIPAA stand for and when was it enacted?
flashcards.back: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act — passed 1996, updated 2003; protects patient privacy while improving the flow of health information.
flashcards.source: HIPAA: Patient Confidentiality (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

flashcards.front: What three rights does HIPAA give patients?
flashcards.back: To request access to their health information, request that providers amend it, and request restrictions on information sharing.
flashcards.source: HIPAA: Patient Confidentiality (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

flashcards.front: As SLPAs/SLPs, what are our core confidentiality duties?
flashcards.back: Treat client info as confidential; don't discuss clients outside the facility; access only info needed for the job; get permission before sharing with anyone; keep files secure.
flashcards.source: HIPAA: Patient Confidentiality (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

flashcards.front: Name four HIPAA-compliant practices.
flashcards.back: Any four: don't share logins/passwords; keep paper files locked; don't travel with files (or protect them completely); don't access info on family/friends; don't store client pictures/info on your phone; don't discuss clients in public; don't approach clients/families in public; don't engage with them on social media.
flashcards.source: HIPAA: Patient Confidentiality (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

flashcards.front: When taking observation notes, how do you protect client identity?
flashcards.back: De-identify individuals — remove names (use initials or an assigned ID #) and site references so no one can be identified.
flashcards.source: HIPAA: Patient Confidentiality (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

flashcards.front: Name Oller's five stages of prelinguistic vocal development.
flashcards.back: (1) Phonation (birth-1mo), (2) Cooing/Gooing (2-3mo), (3) Exploration/Expansion (4-6mo), (4) Canonical babbling (7-9mo), (5) Variegated babbling (10-12mo).
flashcards.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

flashcards.front: In what general order are speech sounds acquired (Sander, 1972)?
flashcards.back: Nasals + stops + glides earliest → fricatives + 'th' → affricates → liquids (l, r). Voiced/voiceless 'th' are generally the latest.
flashcards.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

flashcards.front: Which phonological processes typically DISAPPEAR by age 3?
flashcards.back: Unstressed syllable deletion, final consonant deletion, diminutization, velar fronting, consonant assimilation, reduplication, prevocalic voicing.
flashcards.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

flashcards.front: Which phonological processes typically PERSIST after age 3?
flashcards.back: Cluster reduction, epenthesis, gliding, vocalization, stopping, depalatalization, final consonant devoicing.
flashcards.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

flashcards.front: What is MLU and why does it matter?
flashcards.back: Mean Length of Utterance — the average number of morphemes per utterance; a reliable predictor of language complexity that increases ~1.2 morphemes/year from 18mo to age 5.
flashcards.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

flashcards.front: Brown's Stage I: age, MLU, and milestones?
flashcards.back: 12-26 months; MLU 1.0-2.0; uses 1-, 2-, 3-word utterances, intonation for yes/no questions, limited wh- questions.
flashcards.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

flashcards.front: What are the speech intelligibility expectations by age?
flashcards.back: 19-24mo: 25-50%; 2-3yr: 50-75%; 4-5yr: 75-90%; 5+yr: 90-100% understood by an unfamiliar listener.
flashcards.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

flashcards.front: Which grammatical morphemes emerge earliest (Brown)?
flashcards.back: Present progressive -ing emerges first (19-28mo), then regular plural -s, possessive -'s, and present-tense auxiliaries (29-38mo).
flashcards.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

flashcards.front: Name three red flags for a 12-month-old.
flashcards.back: Does not point to objects; does not use gestures such as waving or shaking head. (Also from nearby ages: limited/no babbling by 9mo, no first word by 15mo.)
flashcards.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

flashcards.front: Red flag at 24 months?
flashcards.back: A vocabulary of fewer than 50 words and/or decreased interest in social interactions.
flashcards.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

flashcards.front: What order do pronouns generally emerge?
flashcards.back: I and it first, then you; most subjective and objective pronouns by age 3 and possessive pronouns by age 5 (Owens).
flashcards.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

flashcards.front: Give an example of velar fronting and when it resolves.
flashcards.back: Velar fronting substitutes a front sound for a back sound (can → /tæn/); fronting of initial velars typically resolves by ~4 years.
flashcards.source: LinguiSystems Guide to Communication Milestones (Lanza & Flahive, 2009)

flashcards.front: What is task analysis?
flashcards.back: Breaking a complex task into smaller, more manageable steps (e.g., spelling your name: learn letters → letters in your name → trace → spell independently).
flashcards.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

flashcards.front: What is scaffolding?
flashcards.back: Support provided in incremental steps to help someone learn a new skill, faded as accuracy increases.
flashcards.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

flashcards.front: How do you set up treatment to keep a client in the ZPD?
flashcards.back: Identify the steps to the goal, determine what the client can do independently, find the next step up (where they need you), use models/prompts/cues to keep them successful, and fade supports as accuracy increases.
flashcards.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

flashcards.front: What two dimensions of complexity does a clinician adjust?
flashcards.back: Linguistic complexity (the language used) and social complexity (the setting) — building a hierarchy of tasks to master.
flashcards.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

flashcards.front: What are the three types of modeling described?
flashcards.back: Modeling with emphasis, modeling for direct imitation, and modeling for delayed imitation — begin with constant models, fade to occasional, then fade completely.
flashcards.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

flashcards.front: What's the difference between a cue and a prompt?
flashcards.back: A cue is a hint (visual, auditory, or tactile) to help the client succeed; a prompt is a question or direction for the client to respond to. Both start frequent and are faded to occasional/subtle.
flashcards.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

flashcards.front: What are the three modalities of cues?
flashcards.back: Visual, auditory, and tactile.
flashcards.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

flashcards.front: What makes feedback most effective?
flashcards.back: It is specific, succinct/quick, and followed by an immediate opportunity to practice; begin with copious feedback and fade to occasional, subtle forms.
flashcards.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

flashcards.front: Specific vs. non-specific feedback — give an example of each (positive).
flashcards.back: Non-specific (evaluative): 'Good job' / 'Nice /s/.' Specific (descriptive): 'You said your /s/ so clearly — you put your tongue behind your front teeth and that sound came right out.'
flashcards.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

flashcards.front: How should supports (models, prompts, cues, feedback) change over time?
flashcards.back: Begin with frequent/copious support and fade to occasional, subtler forms as the client's accuracy and independence grow.
flashcards.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

flashcards.front: What questions guide a task analysis?
flashcards.back: What's the final goal? What must happen first? What are the major steps? Can steps be broken down further? What knowledge/skills, tools, or resources are needed? Where could someone get stuck? How would you know it was completed successfully?
flashcards.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

questions.text: Explain the difference between speech and language, and give one example of a structure or process involved in each.
questions.answer: Speech is the physiological/motor act of producing and manipulating sound (e.g., using the vocal folds, lips, and tongue) — the oral expression of language. Language is a rule-based cognitive system of symbols used to communicate (e.g., applying syntax rules to build a sentence), with expressive and receptive components. Speech is generally considered innate; language is learned.
questions.source: Module 1 Review (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

questions.text: List the four subsystems of speech production in order (from the power source upward) and give the role of each.
questions.answer: 1) Respiration — the power supply (inhalation via thoracic muscles, exhalation via abdominal muscles). 2) Phonation — the noise source (vocal folds of the larynx). 3) Resonation — the tone shapers (pharynx, mouth, nasal cavities). 4) Articulation — the producers of speech sounds (lips, teeth, tongue, alveolar ridge, hard/soft palate, mandible).
questions.source: Hulit, Fahey & Howard (2015), Born to Talk

questions.text: Describe the Bloom & Lahey taxonomy of language, naming all three dimensions and what each contains.
questions.answer: The Bloom & Lahey taxonomy models language as three intersecting dimensions: Form (syntax, morphology, phonology), Content (semantics/meaning), and Use (pragmatics/discourse — the social use of language).
questions.source: Bloom & Lahey (Taxonomy of Language)

questions.answer: Direct supervision is in-view observation and guidance while the SLPA performs a clinical activity (on-site or live telesupervision), allowing immediate feedback — e.g., the SLP observing a therapy session in real time. questions.text: Describe Anderson's Continuum of Supervision, naming its three stages and matching styles.
questions.answer: Anderson's continuum describes how supervision changes as the supervisee gains competence. questions.text: Explain how a clinician uses task analysis and scaffolding to keep a client in their ZPD.
questions.answer: The clinician first performs a task analysis — breaking the goal into smaller steps — and determines what the client can already do independently. They then target the next step up (where the client needs support to succeed) and provide scaffolding using models, prompts, and cues to keep the client successful within the zone of proximal development. As accuracy increases, supports are faded so the client moves toward independence.
questions.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

questions.text: Describe what makes feedback effective and how it should change over the course of therapy.
questions.answer: Effective feedback is specific/descriptive (names exactly what the client did), succinct/quick, and immediately followed by a chance to practice. Clinicians begin with copious feedback and fade to occasional, subtler forms as the client improves. Descriptive feedback ('you put your tongue behind your teeth and that /s/ came right out') is more useful than non-specific evaluative feedback ('good job').
questions.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

questions.text: List the four essential clinical supports and give a strategy example for one.
questions.answer: The four essential clinical supports are: (1) adjust the complexity of the task, (2) use cues/prompts, (3) vary the use of models, and (4) use feedback/reinforcement. Example: for 'adjust complexity,' the clinician builds a hierarchy of tasks varying linguistic and social complexity and moves the client up as they master each level.

notes.title: Module 5 — Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (Study Notes)
notes.body:
STRATEGIES IN SPEECH & LANGUAGE THERAPY — STUDY NOTES
(COMM DIS 3, Module 5)

There are strategies universal in treatment across the practice. Duthie organizes them under the FOUR ESSENTIAL CLINICAL SUPPORTS:
1. Adjust the complexity of the task — Linguistic (language used) and Social (setting) complexity; create a hierarchy of tasks to master as part of the goal.
2. Use cues/prompts.
3. Vary the use of models.
4. Use feedback and/or reinforcement.

======================================================
ZPD — THE TARGET ZONE
======================================================
• The Zone of Proximal Development is the target zone for therapy.
• Set up Tx to keep 'em in the ZPD: identify steps to the goal → what can the client do independently → find the next step up (where they need you) → use models/prompts/cues to keep them successful → fade supports as accuracy increases.

======================================================
TASK ANALYSIS & SCAFFOLDING
======================================================
• TASK ANALYSIS = break a complex task into smaller, more manageable steps.
   Example: spell your name → learn letters → learn the letters in your name → trace the letters → spell on your own.
• SCAFFOLDING = support provided in incremental steps to help someone learn a new skill.
Task-analysis questions: What's the final goal? What must happen first? What are the major steps? Can any step be broken down further? What knowledge/skills are required? What tools/resources are needed? Where could someone get stuck? How would you know it was completed successfully?

======================================================
ADJUST THE COMPLEXITY
======================================================
• LINGUISTIC complexity (language being used) and SOCIAL complexity (setting).
• Create a hierarchy of tasks you want the client to master as part of the goal.

======================================================
MODELING
======================================================
• Modeling, modeling with emphasis
• Modeling for DIRECT imitation
• Modeling for DELAYED imitation
• Begin with constant models → fade to occasional → fade completely.

======================================================
CUES & PROMPTS
======================================================
• CUES = hints to help the client succeed: Visual, Auditory, Tactile.
• PROMPTS = a question or direction for the client to respond to.
• At the beginning: constantly prompting + a variety of cues. Fade to occasional, subtler prompts/cues.

======================================================
FEEDBACK
======================================================
• Provides the client info on their performance.
• Most effective feedback is: SPECIFIC, SUCCINCT/quick, FOLLOWED by an immediate practice opportunity.
• Begin with copious feedback → fade to occasional, subtle forms.
• SPECIFIC (descriptive) beats NON-SPECIFIC (evaluative):
   Positive — Non-specific: 'Good job' / 'Nice /s/.' Specific: 'You said your /s/ so clearly — you put your tongue behind your front teeth and that sound came right out.'
   Corrective — Non-specific: 'No, that is not a good /s/.' Specific: 'Oops, your tongue came between your teeth — can you put it back up to the top of your mouth?'

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
• Four Essential Clinical Supports: adjust complexity, cues/prompts, vary models, feedback/reinforcement.
• Task analysis = break down; Scaffolding = incremental support; Fade as accuracy grows.
• Complexity dimensions: Linguistic + Social → build a task hierarchy.
• Modeling: with emphasis / direct imitation / delayed imitation; constant → faded.
• Cues (visual/auditory/tactile) = hints; Prompts = questions/directions; both faded over time.
• Feedback = specific + succinct + followed by practice; descriptive > evaluative.
notes.source: Strategies in Speech & Language Therapy (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides & notes); Duthie

notes.title: Module 4 — HIPAA & Patient Confidentiality (Study Notes)
notes.body:
HIPAA & PATIENT CONFIDENTIALITY — STUDY NOTES
(COMM DIS 3, Module 4 — for SLPA students and interns)

======================================================
WHAT IS HIPAA?
======================================================
• Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
• Passed 1996, updated 2003
• Purpose: improve the flow of patient health information WHILE protecting patients' privacy rights

HIPAA gives the patient the right to:
• Request access to their health information
• Request that care providers amend their health info
• Request restrictions on information sharing

======================================================
AS SLPAs/SLPs, WE:
======================================================
• Treat info about our patients/clients/students as confidential
• Do NOT discuss them outside of the facility
• Only access medical/background info we NEED to do our job (minimum necessary)
• Seek patient permission before sharing info with ANYONE
• Keep our files secure

======================================================
HIPAA-COMPLIANT PRACTICES
======================================================
• Do not share log-ins/passwords
• Keep paper files in locked cabinets
• Do not travel with files (if you must, protect them with your life)
• Do not access health information on family & friends
• Do not store pictures/info on your phone
• Do not discuss clients in public settings
• Do not approach clients/families in public
• Do not engage with clients/families on social media

======================================================
HIPAA AT DELTA COLLEGE
======================================================
COMM DIS 3: observing therapy (e.g., UOP clinic/CDC) — do NOT discuss the clients you observe;
de-identify individuals in your notes; using names in class is permissible only if the door is shut.
COMM DIS 9 / CDC: use the ID # provided (not the child's name); don't discuss cases outside the CDC and class.
Internship: most rules apply — discuss specifics with your supervisor.

======================================================
IDENTIFY-THE-PROBLEM TAKEAWAYS
======================================================
• Don't show/discuss clinic logs in public (cafe) — even without names.
• Don't greet/approach a client in public (can reveal the clinical relationship).
• Don't photograph clients on a personal phone or email PHI to personal accounts.
• Don't send your clinic log to another provider without proper authorization.
• DO de-identify logs (initials, color-coding for sites) AND get supervisor approval before a traveling-file system.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
• HIPAA = 1996 (updated 2003); protects PHI, gives patients access/amend/restrict rights.
• Minimum necessary: access only what you need.
• De-identify notes; secure all files; never on personal phones/social media/public settings.
notes.source: HIPAA: Patient Confidentiality (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

notes.title: Module 4 — Therapy Approaches (Study Notes)
notes.body:
THERAPY APPROACHES — STUDY NOTES
(COMM DIS 3, Module 4 — An Overview of Tx Approaches)

Therapy approaches fall on a continuum from LEAST NATURAL to MOST NATURAL.
(In Duthie & Reece, the two most-natural approaches are combined and called the "naturalistic approach.")

======================================================
CLINICIAN-DIRECTED APPROACH
======================================================
CHARACTERISTICS:
• Clinician controls the session
• Clinician chooses activities, targets, and determines a successful response
• Clinician often chooses reinforcers
• Clinician elicits very specific responses (imitative or spontaneous)
STRATEGIES: Drill • Drill Play

ADVANTAGES:
• Introducing/teaching a new skill
• Efficient — many repetitions
• Generally easier to plan
• Generally easier to take data
• Works well for articulation, phonology, morphology, syntax

DISADVANTAGES:
• Some clients cannot tolerate it
• Does not follow typical communication patterns
• Language is decontextualized
• Generalization is difficult
• Not great for semantics, pragmatics, fluency

======================================================
NATURALISTIC APPROACH
======================================================
CHARACTERISTICS:
• Treatment happens in the natural environment
• Follows typical communication patterns
• Client plays a role in selecting activities
• Clinician models/stresses targets
• No expectation for a response
STRATEGIES: Indirect language stimulation • Milieu teaching • Script therapy • Focused language stimulation

ADVANTAGES:
• Motivation • Sustained attention • Treatment efficacy
• Caregiver participation/coaching
• Generalization (great for later stages of therapy)
• Great for semantics, pragmatics (contextualized)

DISADVANTAGES:
• Not as efficient at targeting specific responses
• Difficult to get repetitions
• Difficult to plan • Difficult to take data
• Not great for initial stages of articulation/phonology tx

======================================================
HOW TO CHOOSE AN APPROACH
======================================================
Consider: Age of the client • Social abilities of the client • Goals • Where the client is in the therapeutic process

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
• Clinician-directed = clinician controls everything; drill/drill play; efficient; best for artic/phono/morph/syntax; weak generalization.
• Naturalistic = natural environment, child-led, modeling, no demand; best for semantics/pragmatics & generalization; weak for initial artic/phono.
• Choose based on: age, social ability, goals, stage in therapy.
notes.source: An Overview of Tx Approaches (COMM DIS 3 lecture slides)

notes.title: Module 2 — Defining the Roles of SLPAs (Study Notes)
notes.body:
MODULE 2: DEFINING THE ROLES OF SLPAs — STUDY NOTES
(COMM DIS 3 — Scope of Practice, Qualifications, Supervision, Ethics)

======================================================
1. SCOPE OF PRACTICE — WHERE IT COMES FROM
======================================================
• Two authorities define what an SLPA may do:
   - ASHA SLPA Scope of Practice (2022)
   - California: Title 16, Division 13.4, Article 12 (§1399.170 et seq.)
• CA Board / DCA: speechandhearing.ca.gov | ASHA: asha.org/policy/slpa-scope-of-practice
• The SLPA is NOT an independent practitioner and never has their own caseload.

======================================================
2. MINIMUM QUALIFICATIONS FOR THE SUPERVISING SLP
======================================================
• ASHA CCC-SLP (and/or state license)
• Completion of the 9-month Clinical Fellowship (CFY) + experience
• At least 2 hours of CE in clinical instruction/supervision
• Adherence to state laws on SLPA supervision

EXPECTATIONS FOR THE SUPERVISING SLP
• Adhere to Code of Ethics and licensure laws
• Conduct ongoing competency evaluations of the SLPA
• Provide ongoing, caseload-specific training
• Provide treatment plans + assist with implementation
• Provide case management; make all case-management decisions
• Retain legal and ethical responsibility for clients
• COLLABORATE WITH THE SLPA

======================================================
3. ANDERSON'S CONTINUUM OF SUPERVISION
======================================================
STAGES  →  STYLES (supervisor involvement decreases as competence grows):
• Evaluation-Feedback  →  Direct/Active
• Transitional         →  Collaborative
• Self-Supervision      →  Consultative

======================================================
4. TYPES OF SUPERVISION
======================================================
DIRECT
• In-view observation and guidance while the SLPA works (on-site OR live telesupervision)
• Allows immediate feedback
• Reviewing a recording LATER does NOT count as direct

INDIRECT
• SLP not present/reachable in real time
• Examples: reviewing demo videos, client files, recorded sessions; supervisory conferences by phone/secure virtual meeting

IMMEDIATE (California term)
• Required for direct client activity with medically fragile patients; SLPA acts only under the supervisor's direction

======================================================
5. FREQUENCY & AMOUNT OF SUPERVISION
======================================================
FIRST 90 DAYS (after initial licensure):
• California reg: at least 20% per week DIRECT (on-site) supervision
• Course slide: ~30% total supervision, of which ≥20% direct; SLP contact with each student at least every 2 weeks
AFTER 90 DAYS:
• Minimum of 1 hour direct supervision weekly
• 100% direct supervision for medically fragile clients
• Amount, frequency, and type scale with the SLPA's skills and experience
• An SLPA may NOT perform tasks when the SLP cannot be reached by personal contact

SLP-to-SLPA ratio: no more than 3 FTE SLPAs (CA: FTE = ≥30 hrs/week)

======================================================
6. WITHIN vs. OUTSIDE SCOPE
======================================================
WITHIN (with training + supervision):
• Administer/score screenings & assessments (NO interpretation)
• Implement the SLP's documented plan of care
• Provide direct therapy on SLP-developed goals
• Document/collect data; prepare charts and graphs
• Program AAC devices; develop low-tech AAC materials
• Provide caregiver coaching; clerical/admin support

OUTSIDE (never):
• Diagnose disorders; interpret assessments; determine eligibility
• Write, develop, or modify the plan of care
• Make referrals; discharge clients
• Sign formal documents without the SLP's co-signature
• Represent themselves as the SLP
• Select AAC systems/devices
• Treat medically fragile clients without 100% direct supervision
• (CA) Perform high-acumen procedures: vocal tract prosthesis shaping/fitting, vocal tract imaging, oropharyngeal swallow therapy with bolus

======================================================
7. ETHICS — ASHA ASSISTANTS CODE OF CONDUCT (2020)
======================================================
Three Principles of Conduct:
• I. Responsibility to persons served professionally
• II. Responsibility to the public (honesty, no fraud/misrepresentation)
• III. Responsibility for professional relationships (collaboration, no harassment/discrimination, cite sources)
• Assistants are NOT independent practitioners; must be supervised per state law and ASHA's Code.

======================================================
8. CALIFORNIA-SPECIFIC RULES (Article 12)
======================================================
• Name tag: name + registration status in ≥18-point type; self-identify as SLPA
• SLPA limited to duties in B&P Code §2538.1
• Supervisor must hold a current, active, unrestricted CA SLP license and submit a "Responsibility Statement" to the Board within 30 business days of starting supervision
• Outside scope (§1399.170.3): no evaluations, no interpreting data, no altering treatment plans, no signing in lieu of the SLP, no representing self as SLP, no high-acumen procedures

======================================================
9. WORK SETTINGS & DUTIES
======================================================
SETTINGS: public schools (pre-K, K-8, HS, ATP) • private clinics (1:1, small group, ~1-hr sessions) • early intervention (birth-3, home visits, parent coaching)
DUTIES: read/understand goals • plan goal-targeted activities • provide therapy (1:1, small group, push-in) • document services • manage materials • support SLP with clerical work (progress reports, IEP paperwork) • coordinate with teachers & parents

======================================================
★ KEY EXAM POINTS
======================================================
★ SLP supervisor mins: CCC-SLP + 9-mo CFY + 2 hrs supervision CE + state law.
★ Anderson: Evaluation-Feedback/Direct → Transitional/Collaborative → Self-Supervision/Consultative.
★ Direct = in-view + immediate feedback (live telesupervision OK); recorded review = INDIRECT.
★ CA first 90 days: ≥20% direct/week; after 90 days: ≥1 hr direct/week; medically fragile = 100% direct.
★ SLPA may NOT: diagnose, interpret, write/modify plan of care, refer, discharge, sign alone, or self-represent as the SLP.
★ SLP always retains legal + ethical responsibility; SLPA never has an independent caseload.
★ CA name tag: ≥18-point type. FTE = ≥30 hrs/wk; ≤3 FTE SLPAs per SLP.
★ SLPA may not work when the SLP is unreachable.

MODULE 1: COMMUNICATION FOUNDATIONS — STUDY NOTES
(COMM DIS 3: Therapy Analysis and Observations — Week 1 Review)

======================================================
1. WHAT IS COMMUNICATION?
======================================================
• Communication = the process of exchanging information, ideas, thoughts, and feelings.
• Communication can be INTENDED or UNINTENDED.
• Communication methods are ever-changing (speech, writing, gesture, sign, AAC, digital, etc.).

======================================================
2. SPEECH vs. LANGUAGE  (Speech = INNATE  |  Language = LEARNED)
======================================================
SPEECH
• Physiological (motor) process.
• The act of creating and manipulating sound.
• "The oral expression of language."
• Structures: lungs, larynx, oral and nasal structures.

LANGUAGE
• Cognitive process.
• A rule-based system for communicating.
• Has expressive AND receptive components.
• Governed by left-hemisphere brain structures.

======================================================
3. COMMUNICATION FRAMEWORK (components)
======================================================
SPEECH components:      Articulation • Phonology • Fluency • Voice
LANGUAGE components:    Semantics • Morphology • Syntax • Pragmatics

======================================================
4. THE PROCESS OF SPEECH  (Hulit, Fahey & Howard, 2015)
======================================================
Signal flow: BRAIN ("the computer center") coordinates via MOTOR pathways (out) and SENSORY pathways (feedback in).
From the power source upward:

• RESPIRATION — the power supply
    Inhalation: thoracic muscles | Exhalation: abdominal muscles
• PHONATION — the noise source
    Vocal folds of the larynx
• RESONATION — the tone shapers
    Pharynx, mouth, and nasal cavities
• ARTICULATION — the producers of speech sounds
    Lips, teeth, tongue, alveolar ridge, hard palate, soft palate, and mandible

Three speech-production subsystems (Kent, 1997):
• Supralaryngeal / pharyngeal-oral-nasal system (upper airway): nasal cavity, oral cavity, pharyngeal cavity, lips, tongue, jaw
• Laryngeal system: the larynx
• Respiratory system: trachea and lungs

======================================================
5. EXPRESSIVE vs. RECEPTIVE LANGUAGE
======================================================
RECEPTIVE (Comprehension):   Listening • Reading
EXPRESSIVE (Production):      Speaking • Writing

======================================================
6. BLOOM & LAHEY TAXONOMY OF LANGUAGE  (Form ∩ Content ∩ Use)
======================================================
• FORM — Syntax, Morphology, Phonology
• CONTENT — Semantics
• USE — Pragmatics / Discourse

======================================================
7. THE SPEECH CHAIN  (Denes & Pinson, 1973)
======================================================
The forms a spoken message takes from the speaker's mind to the listener's mind:
• Speaker: BRAIN → motor nerves → vocal muscles → sound waves
• Listener: ear → sensory nerves → BRAIN
• A FEEDBACK LINK lets the speaker monitor their own output.
Levels the message passes through:
   Linguistic → Physiological → Acoustic → Physiological → Linguistic

======================================================
8. AUDITORY FEEDBACK LOOP
======================================================
I say it → I hear it → I process it → I modify it → (repeat)

======================================================
★ KEY EXAM POINTS
======================================================
★ Speech = physiological/motor & innate; Language = cognitive & learned.
★ Speech components: Articulation, Phonology, Fluency, Voice.
★ Language components: Semantics, Morphology, Syntax, Pragmatics.
★ Process of speech (bottom-up): Respiration → Phonation → Resonation → Articulation.
★ Match the "role" phrases: power supply / noise source / tone shapers / producers of speech sounds.
★ Receptive = listening + reading (comprehension); Expressive = speaking + writing (production).
★ Bloom & Lahey: FORM (syntax/morphology/phonology), CONTENT (semantics), USE (pragmatics).
★ Language is left-hemisphere.
★ The Speech Chain levels: Linguistic → Physiological → Acoustic → Physiological → Linguistic.
★ Auditory feedback loop: say → hear → process → modify.
